data.text: Metro Manila air quality ‘still not normal’ due to Navotas landfill fire — PhilSA https://t.co/BGFi7Q8w01

Apocalypse Warning - READ IT THROUGH 🚨🚨🚨

We are in the beginning stages of an apocalypse.

 Iran has banned ships from the UK, India, Canada, Australia, the UAE, US, Japan and the EU from using the Strait of Hormuz. The US has a blockade. The Middle East is in turmoil. There is no end in sight.

Oil refineries have mysteriously been catching fire all over the world.

UN says this ban could push 45 million people into hunger.

The IEA says the world is having the worst energy crisis in history.

The middle class is about to be wiped out.

This is just Phase 1.

Take a closer look at what's going on...

Gasoline, diesel, and other fuels: Long queues and panic buying in Vietnam, India, Bangladesh, Philippines, Myanmar, Thailand, Indonesia, Kenya, and parts of Australia. Rationing or self-imposed limits at stations in South Africa, Philippines (national energy emergency declared), and elsewhere. Some countries report only weeks of reserves.

Jet fuel (aviation fuel): Severe disruptions expected or already hitting airlines. Flight cancellations, route cuts, and surcharges in Asia/Oceania; Europe risks acute shortages within weeks (IEA warnings). Prices have more than doubled in some markets.

Natural Gas and LNG

Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) and natural gas: Qatar declared force majeure and shut down some liquefaction plants; Iran attacks reduced output. Spot prices in Asia surged over 140%, Europe’s prices nearly doubled. This affects power generation, industry, and heating. Countries like Bangladesh and India have curtailed industrial use or closed facilities.

3. Fertilizers (Urea, Ammonia, Nitrogen-Based)
Major Gulf producers (which supply ~1/3 of global seaborne fertilizer trade) are blocked. Many fertilizer plants worldwide have shut or slowed due to high gas prices.

Direct impact: Urea prices up sharply; farmers in the U.S., Australia, India, Europe, and developing countries face shortages during key planting seasons.

Ripple effect: Threatens food security and higher food prices later in 2026 (wheat, rice, corn, etc.). UN agencies warn this is a top concern for developing countries

Petrochemicals and Plastics (Turning into an “Everything Crisis”) Oil and gas are feedstocks for thousands of everyday products. Shortages of naphtha, methanol, and related chemicals are causing:
Plastics for packaging (noodles, rice, snacks, bottled water, trash bags, vacuum-sealed bags).
Polyester chips for fabrics/clothing, adhesives, solvents, industrial lubricants.
Medical items (hemodialysis tubes, medical gloves, syringes).

Other consumer goods (condoms, cosmetics packaging, toys).

Prices for plastic resins in Asia have risen 50–59% in some cases; manufacturers in South Korea, Taiwan, Japan, India, China, Thailand, and Indonesia are running low on stocks or halting production.

Other Notable Shortages and Impacts

Aluminum and energy-intensive metals: Gulf smelters hit hard → supply crunches for manufacturing.

Helium: ~1/3 of global supply disrupted (Qatar) → affects semiconductors (chips for electronics/AI), MRIs, and aerospace.

Electricity/power:  Rolling blackouts or conservation measures in Bangladesh (universities/shopping centres closed early), India (risk of summer power shortages), South Sudan, and parts of Southeast Asia. Some countries are ramping up coal use as a stopgap.

DISASTER RESPONSE UPDATE| BFP, JICA Lead Coordinated Action Planning for Navotas Landfill Incident

The Bureau of Fire Protection, led by its Officer-in-Charge, Fire Chief Superintendent Wilberto Rico Neil A Kwan Tiu, took part in the kickoff meeting, action planning session for Navotas Sanitary Landfill in collaboration with the Japan International Cooperation Agency and key Philippine government agencies, earlier today. 

The activity brought together representatives from the Office of Civil Defense, Department of Environment and Natural Resources, Armed Forces of the Philippines, and other stakeholders to strengthen coordination and develop responsive strategies for the ongoing incident.

Source: Bureau of Fire
